steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine learning paper on quantized (further tensorized) Fourier and polynomial features for tensor network kernel models. Set up kernel machines with tensor-product features and their scaling problems, review low-rank and tensor network approaches, and state what our quantized representation achieves, with a numbered list of the experimental findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Supervised learning with kernel machines and feature maps
- Tensor-product features and their exponential scaling
- Dual formulation and low-rank kernel approximations
- Tensor network constraints on the weights
- Our contribution: exact quantized features and weights; expressiveness
- Experimental findings (numbered)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Setup
  - supervised learning: estimate f\left(\cdot\right):\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y} from N pairs \left\{\bm{x}_{n},y_{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{N}
  - kernel machines: lift data via feature map \bm{z}\left(\cdot\right):\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}, linear relationship there
  - training: minimize regularized empirical risk with convex loss \ell\left(\cdot,\cdot\right):\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}% _{+}
  - loss choice -> different kernel machine: squared loss = KRR (cite), hinge = SVMs (cite), logistic = logistic regression
  - feature map choice -> different nonlinear behaviors
- Tensor-product features
  - \bm{v}^{(d)}(\cdot):\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{M_{d}} on each component x_{d} of \bm{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{D}; \otimes = left Kronecker product (cite)
  - arise in product kernels (cite), Fourier features (cite), B-splines (cite), polynomials (cite)
  - exponentially large feature vector \bm{z}(\bm{x})\in\mathbb{C}^{M_{1}M_{2}\cdots M_{D}}; exponential number of weights \bm{w}
  - limits to low-dimensional data or very low degree mappings
- Dual formulation
  - kernel function k(\bm{x},\bm{x^{\prime}})=\left\langle\bm{z}(\bm{x}),\bm{z}(\bm{x^{\prime}})\right\rangle; pairwise similarity
  - kernel matrix \mathcal{O}(N^{2}); N Lagrange multipliers, convex quadratic problem, at least \mathcal{O}(N^{2}); no large N
  - low-rank kernel approximations: polynomial sketching (cite), random features (cite); probabilistic guarantees
- Tensor networks
  - tensor network constraint on \bm{w} (cite)
  - polyadic rank- R: storage \mathcal{O}(M^{D}) -> \mathcal{O}(DMR); \mathcal{O}(DMR) per gradient descent iteration
  - explored for polynomial (cite), pure-power- 1 polynomials (cite), higher-degree pure-power (cite), B-splines (cite), Fourier features (cite)
- Contribution
  - exact quantized representation (cite) of pure-power polynomials and Fourier features via Vandermonde structure
  - quantized = further tensorized, not lower precision floating point
  - quantize model weights; no additional computational cost; same exact features
  - same number of parameters -> higher upper bounds on VC-dimension -> potentially more expressive; bounds not necessarily met in practice
- Findings
  - 1. higher expressiveness: section 5.1, underparameterized regime, lower test errors with identical features and parameter count
  - 2. regularization: peaks of frequency spectrum learned first (Fourier features), section 5.2; most salient features first
  - 3. state-of-the-art on large-scale real-life problems, section 5.3; vs non-quantized and other methods; superior generalization on a laptop computer

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In supervised learning, the goal is to estimate a function f\left(\cdot\right):\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y} given N input-output pairs \left\{\bm{x}_{n},y_{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{N}, where \bm{x}\in\mathcal{X} and y\in\mathcal{Y}. Kernel machines do this by lifting the input data into a high-dimensional feature space with a feature map \bm{z}\left(\cdot\right):\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{H} and then looking for a linear relationship in that space:

Training this kind of model means minimizing the regularized empirical risk for a convex measure of loss \ell\left(\cdot,\cdot\right):\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}% _{+}

Choosing different losses gives the primal formulation of different kernel machines. For example, squared loss gives kernel ridge regression (KRR), hinge loss gives support vector machines (SVMs), and logistic loss gives logistic regression. Choosing different feature maps \bm{z} lets us model different nonlinear behaviors in the data. In this article we consider tensor-product features

where \bm{v}^{(d)}(\cdot):\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{M_{d}} is a feature map that acts on each element of the d -th component x_{d} of \bm{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{D}. Here \otimes is the left Kronecker product. This tensor-product structure comes up with product kernels, Fourier features, B-splines and polynomials.

Because of the tensor-product structure in equation 3, \bm{z}(\cdot) maps an input sample \bm{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{D} into a feature vector \bm{z}(\bm{x})\in\mathbb{C}^{M_{1}M_{2}\cdots M_{D}} that is exponentially large. So the model also has an exponential number of weights \bm{w}. This exponential scaling of the number of features means that tensor-product features can only be used for low-dimensional data or for mappings of very low degree.

You can avoid both of these computational limitations completely with the dual formulation of the learning problem in equation 2, where you have to compute the pairwise similarity of all the data with a kernel function k(\bm{x},\bm{x^{\prime}})=\left\langle\bm{z}(\bm{x}),\bm{z}(\bm{x^{\prime}})\right\rangle. But the dual formulation needs the kernel matrix, which costs \mathcal{O}(N^{2}), and it needs to estimate N Lagrange multipliers by solving a (convex) quadratic problem, which costs at least \mathcal{O}(N^{2}), so large-scale data (large N) cannot be handled. To get around this, a lot of research has looked for low-rank approximations of kernels with random methods such as polynomial sketching and random features, which approximate the feature space with probabilistic approximation guarantees.

Another way to use the tensor-product structure in equation 3 is to put a tensor network constraint on the weights \bm{w}. For example, a polyadic rank- R constraint reduces the storage complexity of the weights from \mathcal{O}(M^{D}) to \mathcal{O}(DMR) and makes it possible to develop efficient learning algorithms with computational complexity \mathcal{O}(DMR) per gradient descent iteration. This has been explored for polynomial pure-power- 1 polynomials, pure-power polynomials of higher degree, B-splines, and Fourier features.

In this article we improve on all of this research by deriving an exact quantized representation of pure-power polynomials and Fourier features, using their Vandermonde structure. Note that in this paper quantized means further tensorized, and it is not the same as working with lower precision floating point numbers. Because we have the quantized features, we can quantize the model weights. We show that quantized models can be trained with no additional computational cost compared to non-quantized ones, while learning from exactly the same features. Most importantly, with the same number of model parameters, the quantized models have higher upper bounds on the VC-dimension, which means they could be more expressive. These bounds are not necessarily met in practice, but we verify experimentally that:

- 1. Quantized models really are more expressive. We show this in section 5.1, where in the underparameterized regime quantized models get lower test errors than non-quantized models with identical features and identical total number of model parameters.

- 2. The extra structure regularizes the problem, because it prioritizes learning the peaks in the frequency spectrum of the signal (for Fourier features) (section 5.2). So the quantized structure learns the most salient features in the data first with the limited number of model parameters it has.

- 3. Quantized tensor network models can give state-of-the-art performance on large-scale real-life problems. We show this in section 5.3, where we compare the proposed quantized model to its non-quantized counterpart and to other state-of-the-art methods, and it has superior generalization performance on a laptop computer.

For example, a polyadic rank- R constraint reduces the storage complexity of the weights from \mathcal{O}(M^{D}) down to \mathcal{O}(DMR) and enables efficient learning algorithms with a computational complexity of \mathcal{O}(DMR) per gradient descent iteration. This idea has been explored for polynomial [17,18,19,20,21] pure-power- 1 polynomials [22], pure-power polynomials of higher degree [23], B-splines [8], and Fourier features [7,24,25,26,27,28].

In this article, we improve on this entire line of research by deriving an exact quantized representation [29] of pure-power polynomials and Fourier features that exploits their inherent Vandermonde structure. Note that in this paper quantized means further tensorized, and should not be confused with working with lower precision floating point numbers. Thanks to the derived quantized features, we are able to quantize the model weights. We show that, compared to their non-quantized counterparts, quantized models can be trained at no additional computational cost while learning from exactly the same features. Most importantly, for the same number of model parameters, the resulting quantized models have higher upper bounds on the VC-dimension, which indicates potentially higher expressiveness. While these bounds are not necessarily met in practice, we verify experimentally that:

- 1. Quantized models are indeed more expressive. This is demonstrated in section 5.1, where we show that in the underparameterized regime quantized models achieve lower test errors than non-quantized models with identical features and an identical total number of model parameters.

- 2. This additional structure regularizes the problem by prioritizing the learning of the peaks in the frequency spectrum of the signal (in the case of Fourier features) (section 5.2). In other words, the quantized structure learns the most salient features in the data first with its limited number of available model parameters.

- 3. Quantized tensor network models can deliver state-of-the-art performance on large-scale real-life problems. This is demonstrated in section 5.3, where we compare the proposed quantized model to both its non-quantized counterpart and other state-of-the-art methods, showing superior generalization performance on a laptop computer.
